claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating grid-like codes in various domains.

claims.claim: The social value map was defined by two ecologically important dimensions: competence and trustworthiness.
claims.source: We designed the social value map, an abstract social space structuring one's social perception of other people's social values. It was defined by two ecologically important dimensions: competence and trustworthiness.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claims.claim: Competence was operationally defined as the ability to earn a profit (profit rate) in an investment game.
claims.source: We operationally defined these two dimensions under the framework of an investment game, in which the trustee's social value is determined by the ability to earn a profit (i.e., profit rate as competence) and the proportion of earnings returned to the investor (i.e., return rate as trustworthiness).
claims.evidence: This describes the operational definition used in the study.

claims.claim: Trustworthiness was operationally defined as the proportion of earnings returned to the investor (return rate) in an investment game.
claims.source: We operationally defined these two dimensions under the framework of an investment game, in which the trustee's social value is determined by the ability to earn a profit (i.e., profit rate as competence) and the proportion of earnings returned to the investor (i.e., return rate as trustworthiness).
claims.evidence: This describes the operational definition used in the study.

claims.claim: Six avatars with different levels of competence and trustworthiness were placed on the social value map.
claims.source: Six avatars with different levels of competence and trustworthiness (Figure 1A), analogous to landmarks in the physical environment, were placed on the social value map of size 1 unit × 1 unit in accordance with the range of competence and trustworthiness.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design, with reference to Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Participants were successful in reconstructing the designed layout of avatars in a map task at the end of the experiment.
claims.source: Participants were successful in reconstructing the designed layout of avatars in a map task at the end of the experiment (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a behavioral result from the study, with reference to Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Participants took significantly less time to find all avatars in the review session compared to the learning session.
claims.source: In the explore task, it took them significantly less time to find all avatars in the review session compared to the learning session (βsession = –67.589, t = –37.604, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from linear mixed effect models.

claims.claim: Participants spent much less time at the edge during exploration in the review session compared to the learning session.
claims.source: They also spent much less time at the edge (β = –0.104, t = –9.070, p<0.001) and more time at avatars (βsession = 0.023, t = 7.367, p<0.001) during exploration in the review session compared to the learning session (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from linear mixed effect models, with reference to Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Participants spent more time at avatars during exploration in the review session compared to the learning session.
claims.source: They also spent much less time at the edge (β = –0.104, t = –9.070, p<0.001) and more time at avatars (βsession = 0.023, t = 7.367, p<0.001) during exploration in the review session compared to the learning session (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from linear mixed effect models, with reference to Figure 1E.

claims.claim: There was evident improvement in collect and recall task as training progressed.
claims.source: Likewise, there was evident improvement in collect and recall task as training progressed (Figure 1F, percentage of first transition deviation < 15° in collect task: βsession = 0.050411, t = 3.2187, p=0.002; percentage of distance < 0.01 in collect task: βsession = 0.047, t = 3.002, p=0.003; accuracy in the recall task: βsession = 0.020, t = 4.213, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from linear mixed effect models, with reference to Figure 1F.

claims.claim: There was a significant effect of distance between avatars in the compared dimension on response time and accuracy in the compare task.
claims.source: In the compare task, linear mixed effect models revealed a significant effect of distance between avatars in the compared dimension on response time and accuracy as predicted (Figure 2G, all p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from linear mixed effect models, with reference to Figure 2G (note: this appears to be Figure 1G based on context).

claims.claim: Learning induced changes in participants' ratings of avatars on all rating items (competence, trustworthiness, and attractiveness).
claims.source: Lastly, learning-induced changes in participants' ratings of avatars on all rating items (competence, trustworthiness, and attractiveness) (Figure 2H, Table 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the study, with reference to Figure 2H (note: this appears to be Figure 1H based on context) and Table 1A.

claims.claim: There was no preference over the six presented faces when participants were naïve to the social value of different avatars.
claims.source: There was no preference over the six presented faces when participants were naïve to the social value of different avatars (Table 1B, all p>0.890), but their ratings became significantly dissociable according to the learned social value at the end of the experiment (Table 1B, all p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the study, with reference to Table 1B.

claims.claim: Participants' ratings became significantly dissociable according to the learned social value at the end of the experiment.
claims.source: There was no preference over the six presented faces when participants were naïve to the social value of different avatars (Table 1B, all p>0.890), but their ratings became significantly dissociable according to the learned social value at the end of the experiment (Table 1B, all p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the study, with reference to Table 1B.

claims.claim: Activity in the bilateral precuneus positively correlated with traveled Euclidean distance.
claims.source: This analysis revealed two marginally significant clusters in the precuneus whose activity positively correlated with traveled distance on the social value map (Figure 2A, Table 2A, right precuneus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [12, –56, 26], t(37) = 4.952, p=0.056 FWE-corrected; left precuneus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [-12, –54, 18], t(37) = 4.530, p=0.058 FWE-corrected; cluster-defining threshold p<0.001 FWE-corrected).
claims.evidence: This is a result from whole-brain GLM analysis, with reference to Figure 2A and Table 2A.

claims.claim: Negative correlation was observed between traveled distance and activity of clusters in bilateral fusiform gyrus.
claims.source: Interestingly, we also observed negative correlation between traveled distance and activity of clusters in several regions, including bilateral fusiform gyrus (Figure 2B, Table 2B, right fusiform: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [36, –48, –20], t(37) = 5.912, p<0.001 FWE-corrected; left fusiform: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–38, –56, –10], t(37) = 4.724, p=0.008 FWE-corrected) and the right middle occipital gyrus (Figure 2B, Table 2B, peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [34, –68, 20], t(37) = 4.649, p=0.018 FWE-corrected; cluster-defining threshold p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a result from whole-brain GLM analysis, with reference to Figure 2B and Table 2B.

claims.claim: Negative correlation was observed between traveled distance and activity in the right middle occipital gyrus.
claims.source: Interestingly, we also observed negative correlation between traveled distance and activity of clusters in several regions, including bilateral fusiform gyrus (Figure 2B, Table 2B, right fusiform: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [36, –48, –20], t(37) = 5.912, p<0.001 FWE-corrected; left fusiform: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–38, –56, –10], t(37) = 4.724, p=0.008 FWE-corrected) and the right middle occipital gyrus (Figure 2B, Table 2B, peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [34, –68, 20], t(37) = 4.649, p=0.018 FWE-corrected; cluster-defining threshold p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a result from whole-brain GLM analysis, with reference to Figure 2B and Table 2B.

claims.claim: Grid consistency effect was found in bilateral ventral medial PFC aligned to the right FP grid orientation.
claims.source: For the right FP grid orientation, whole-brain analysis revealed consistency effect in bilateral ventral medial PFC (vmPFC, Figure 3D, left and middle panels, peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–14, 56, –12], t(37) = 4.245, cluster-level p=0.033 FWE-corrected, cluster-defining threshold p<0.005) and the left EC (left EC) extending to the parahippocampus (Figure 3E, left and middle panels, peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–16, –22, –26], t(37) = 4.563, cluster-level p=0.024 FWE-corrected, cluster-defining threshold p<0.005).
claims.evidence: This is a result from whole-brain analysis of grid consistency, with reference to Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Grid consistency effect was found in the left EC extending to the parahippocampus aligned to the right FP grid orientation.
claims.source: For the right FP grid orientation, whole-brain analysis revealed consistency effect in bilateral ventral medial PFC (vmPFC, Figure 3D, left and middle panels, peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–14, 56, –12], t(37) = 4.245, cluster-level p=0.033 FWE-corrected, cluster-defining threshold p<0.005) and the left EC (left EC) extending to the parahippocampus (Figure 3E, left and middle panels, peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–16, –22, –26], t(37) = 4.563, cluster-level p=0.024 FWE-corrected, cluster-defining threshold p<0.005).
claims.evidence: This is a result from whole-brain analysis of grid consistency, with reference to Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Significant consistency effect was found in two clusters in bilateral vmPFC aligned to the right pmEC grid orientation.
claims.source: For the right pmEC grid orientation, significant consistency effect was found in two clusters in bilateral vmPFC (Figure 3F, left and middle panels, right rectus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [10, 34, –18], t(37) = 4.908, cluster-level p=0.033 FWE-corrected; left ACC: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–8, 32, 6], t(37) = 4.810, cluster-level p=0.009 FWE-corrected; cluster-defining threshold p<0.005) and one cluster in right superior temporal pole (right STP, Figure 3G, left and middle panels, peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [36, 20, –30], t(37) = 4.962, cluster-level p=0.018 FWE-corrected, cluster-defining threshold p<0.005).
claims.evidence: This is a result from whole-brain analysis of grid consistency, with reference to Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Significant consistency effect was found in one cluster in right superior temporal pole aligned to the right pmEC grid orientation.
claims.source: For the right pmEC grid orientation, significant consistency effect was found in two clusters in bilateral vmPFC (Figure 3F, left and middle panels, right rectus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [10, 34, –18], t(37) = 4.908, cluster-level p=0.033 FWE-corrected; left ACC: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–8, 32, 6], t(37) = 4.810, cluster-level p=0.009 FWE-corrected; cluster-defining threshold p<0.005) and one cluster in right superior temporal pole (right STP, Figure 3G, left and middle panels, peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [36, 20, –30], t(37) = 4.962, cluster-level p=0.018 FWE-corrected, cluster-defining threshold p<0.005).
claims.evidence: This is a result from whole-brain analysis of grid consistency, with reference to Figure 3G.

claims.claim: The study did not identify grid-like pattern in EC that is aligned to the grid orientation of itself.
claims.source: The above analysis did not identify grid-like pattern in EC that is aligned to the grid orientation of itself.
claims.evidence: This is a null finding reported in the results.

claims.claim: The study failed to find evidence of grid-like code in the EC aligned to its own putative grid orientation with the orientation estimation approach or with the RSA approach.
claims.source: However, in the more statistically lenient ROI-based analysis, we failed to find evidence of grid-like code in the EC aligned to its own putative grid orientation either with this orientation estimation approach or with the representation similarity analysis (RSA) approach ('Materials and methods', Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is a null finding reported in the results, with reference to supplementary figures.

claims.claim: A clustered distribution of voxel-wise grid orientations was revealed in FP ROI for each participant.
claims.source: This revealed a clustered distribution of voxel-wise grid orientations in FP ROI (V-test, all p<0.011, except in one participant's estimating set p=0.176; see Figure 3—figure supplement 3A for representative participants).
claims.evidence: This is a result from V-test analysis, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: Grid orientations across participants in the right FP ROI tend to distribute uniformly.
claims.source: Previous studies using a similar approach in fMRI have also shown that grid orientations across participants tend to distribute uniformly (Bao et al., 2019). This has been replicated in the right FP ROI in our dataset (Figure 3—figure supplement 4, top, Rayleigh's tests for nonuniformity, all p>0.782).
claims.evidence: This is a result from Rayleigh's test, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and citation to Bao et al., 2019.

claims.claim: In the pmEC ROI, 31 participants show clustered distribution of voxel-wise orientations.
claims.source: However, in the pmEC ROI, these results are less consistent. With regard to voxel-wise orientations, 31 participants show the above clustered distribution (V-test, all p<0.040; see Figure 3—figure supplement 3B for representative participants), but there are seven participants each of whom has at least one estimating set that did not pass the statistical test (V-test, all p>0.068).
claims.evidence: This is a result from V-test analysis, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: Across participants, only grid orientations from two estimating sets in pmEC ROI conformed to the uniform distribution.
claims.source: Across participants, only grid orientations from two estimating sets conformed to the uniform distribution (Figure 3—figure supplement 4, bottom panel, Rayleigh's tests for nonuniformity, run 1,2,3: p=0.010, run 1,2,4: p=0.019).
claims.evidence: This is a result from Rayleigh's test, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Signals within clusters showing significant hexagonal consistency were not modulated by any of the controlled periodicities (fourfold, fivefold, sevenfold, and eightfold).
claims.source: One-sample t-tests showed that signals within these clusters were not modulated by any of the controlled periodicities, and paired t-test showed that sixfold periodicity in general showed greater alignment effect (Figure 3D–G, right panels).
claims.evidence: This is a result from statistical tests, with reference to Figure 3D-G.

claims.claim: Sixfold periodicity in general showed greater alignment effect compared to controlled periodicities.
claims.source: One-sample t-tests showed that signals within these clusters were not modulated by any of the controlled periodicities, and paired t-test showed that sixfold periodicity in general showed greater alignment effect (Figure 3D–G, right panels).
claims.evidence: This is a result from paired t-tests, with reference to Figure 3D-G.

claims.claim: The vmPFC showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right FP's grid orientation.
claims.source: In sum, our univariate analysis revealed that the vmPFC and left EC showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right FP's grid orientation and that the vmPFC and right STP showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right pmEC's grid orientation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the univariate analysis results.

claims.claim: The left EC showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right FP's grid orientation.
claims.source: In sum, our univariate analysis revealed that the vmPFC and left EC showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right FP's grid orientation and that the vmPFC and right STP showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right pmEC's grid orientation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the univariate analysis results.

claims.claim: The vmPFC showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right pmEC's grid orientation.
claims.source: In sum, our univariate analysis revealed that the vmPFC and left EC showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right FP's grid orientation and that the vmPFC and right STP showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right pmEC's grid orientation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the univariate analysis results.

claims.claim: The right STP showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right pmEC's grid orientation.
claims.source: In sum, our univariate analysis revealed that the vmPFC and left EC showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right FP's grid orientation and that the vmPFC and right STP showed sixfold-specific grid-like code aligned to the right pmEC's grid orientation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the univariate analysis results.

claims.claim: The study did not find correlation between hexagonal modulation effect and accuracy in the recall task in the scanner.
claims.source: Previous studies have found that hexagonal modulation effect and hexagonal consistency effect positively correlate with accuracy in the recall task in the scanner (Constantinescu et al., 2016). However, we did not find such a correlation in our data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a null finding reported in the results, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citation to Constantinescu et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Hexagonal consistency effect in the left middle temporal gyrus correlated with the distance effect in response time for grid orientation of right FP ROI.
claims.source: For grid orientation of right FP ROI (Figure 4A), hexagonal consistency effect in the left middle temporal gyrus and right lingual gyrus correlated with the distance effect (left middle temporal gyrus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–36, –70, 8], t(37) = 4.528, cluster-level p<0.001 FWE-corrected; right lingual gyrus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–38, –66, 4], t(37) = 4.369, cluster-level p<0.001 FWE-corrected; cluster-defining threshold p<0.005).
claims.evidence: This is a result from whole-brain analysis, with reference to Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Hexagonal consistency effect in the right lingual gyrus correlated with the distance effect in response time for grid orientation of right FP ROI.
claims.source: For grid orientation of right FP ROI (Figure 4A), hexagonal consistency effect in the left middle temporal gyrus and right lingual gyrus correlated with the distance effect (left middle temporal gyrus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–36, –70, 8], t(37) = 4.528, cluster-level p<0.001 FWE-corrected; right lingual gyrus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–38, –66, 4], t(37) = 4.369, cluster-level p<0.001 FWE-corrected; cluster-defining threshold p<0.005).
claims.evidence: This is a result from whole-brain analysis, with reference to Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Hexagonal consistency effect in bilateral lingual gyrus correlated with the distance effect for grid orientation of right pmEC ROI.
claims.source: For grid orientation of right pmEC ROI (Figure 4B), hexagonal consistency effect in bilateral lingual correlated with the distance effect (left lingual gyrus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [–12, –68, –2], t(37) = 4.355, cluster-level p=0.077 FWE-corrected; right lingual gyrus: peak coordinate [x, y, z] = [16, –62, –2], t(37) = 3.934, cluster-level p=0.032 FWE-corrected; cluster-defining threshold p<0.005).
claims.evidence: This is a result from whole-brain analysis, with reference to Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Activities in the bilateral precuneus were positively correlated with traveled distance during mental traversal of a predefined social value map.
claims.source: When participants were mentally traversing a predefined social value map, we found that activities in the bilateral precuneus were positively correlated with traveled distance, while activities in bilateral FFG and right MOG were negatively correlated with traveled distance.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the distance coding results in the Discussion.

claims.claim: Activities in bilateral FFG and right MOG were negatively correlated with traveled distance during mental traversal of a predefined social value map.
claims.source: When participants were mentally traversing a predefined social value map, we found that activities in the bilateral precuneus were positively correlated with traveled distance, while activities in bilateral FFG and right MOG were negatively correlated with traveled distance.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the distance coding results in the Discussion.

claims.claim: Precuneus activity was positively correlated with traveled Euclidean distance during implicit navigation in the abstract social space.
claims.source: Likewise, we showed that precuneus activity was positively correlated with traveled Euclidean distance during implicit navigation in the abstract social space.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the distance coding results in the Discussion.

claims.claim: The current study's peak coordinates in precuneus coincide with those reported in a previous study by Park et al., 2020.
claims.source: Moreover, the present peak coordinates coincide with those reported in a previous study by Park et al., 2020.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature, citing Park et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Bilateral precuneus represented pairwise difference in the task-relevant dimension instead of pairwise Euclidean distance in the 2D space in Park et al., 2020 study.
claims.source: In their study, participants learned 2D social hierarchy (competence and popularity) of two groups of agents and were asked to perform a transitive inference task in which they compared a pair of agents on their competence or popularity. The authors found that bilateral precuneus represented pairwise difference in the task-relevant dimension instead of pairwise Euclidean distance in the 2D space.
claims.evidence: This is a description of findings from Park et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Posterior cingulate cortex/precuneus tracks the length of the vector of social relationship change, that is, an egocentric distance.
claims.source: Another study reported that posterior cingulate cortex/precuneus tracks the length of the vector of social relationship change, that is, an egocentric distance (Tavares et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a description of findings from Tavares et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Precuneus may encode the distance of the route, either on a concrete or an abstract map, that participants trespass under task demand.
claims.source: Taken together, we speculate that precuneus may encode the distance of the route, either on a concrete or an abstract map, that participants trespass under task demand.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings in the Discussion.

claims.claim: The current study partly replicated findings of hexagonal modulated pattern in the EC and medial prefrontal regions aligned to putative grid orientation from both regions, with most findings in the prefrontal region.
claims.source: Previous studies on reporting grid-like codes mostly report hexagonal modulated pattern in the EC and medial prefrontal regions aligned to putative grid orientation from both regions (Constantinescu et al., 2016). The current study partly replicated these findings, most of which are in the prefrontal region.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the grid-like code findings in the Discussion, with citation to Constantinescu et al., 2016.

claims.claim: In terms of prefrontal orientation, whole-brain analysis revealed alignment effects in the bilateral vmPFC and left EC.
claims.source: In terms of prefrontal orientation, whole-brain analysis revealed alignment effects in the bilateral vmPFC and left EC.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the grid-like code findings in the Discussion.

claims.claim: In terms of entorhinal orientation, alignment effect was found in the bilateral vmPFC and right superior temporal pole, but not in the EC.
claims.source: In terms of entorhinal orientation, however, alignment effect was found in the bilateral vmPFC and right superior temporal pole, but not in the EC.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the grid-like code findings in the Discussion.

claims.claim: There has been no significant evidence of grid-like neuronal tuning in the prefrontal area to date.
claims.source: To date, there has been no significant evidence of grid-like neuronal tuning in this area (Wikenheiser et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the literature, citing Wikenheiser et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Jacobs et al., 2013 examined grid-like cells in a variety of brain regions, including the frontal cortex in neurosurgical patients during a virtual navigation task, but the proportion of significant grid-like cells in the frontal cortex did not exceed type I error rate.
claims.source: Jacobs et al., 2013 examined grid-like cells in a variety of brain regions, including the frontal cortex in neurosurgical patients during a virtual navigation task, but the proportion of significant grid-like cells in the frontal cortex did not exceed type I error rate (they did identify grid-like cells in cingulate cortex, which is posterior to the prefrontal regions).
claims.evidence: This is a description of findings from Jacobs et al., 2013.

claims.claim: It is less likely that the prefrontal grid-like codes reported in this study and previous literature come from grid cells in the PFC.
claims.source: Therefore, it is less likely that the prefrontal grid-like codes reported in our study and previous literature come from grid cells in the PFC.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of evidence for grid cells in PFC.

claims.claim: A more plausible explanation is that the anatomically and functionally connected medial- and orbitofrontal cortex and EC coordinated together to support flexible decision-making.
claims.source: A more plausible explanation is that the anatomically and functionally connected medial- and orbitofrontal cortex and EC (Navarro Schröder et al., 2015; Peng et al., 2018; Squire and Zola, 1996) coordinated together to support flexible decision-making.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation with citations to support anatomical and functional connectivity.

claims.claim: The current study did not find reliable effect of hexagonal grid-like code in the entorhinal region aligned to its own grid orientation using both univariate and multivariate approaches.
claims.source: However, adopting both univariate and multivariate approaches, the current study did not find the reliable effect of hexagonal grid-like code in the entorhinal region aligned to its own grid orientation, which should be evident if such hypothesis stands.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the null finding in EC.

claims.claim: Previous studies postulated that the lack of univariate evidence of grid-like code may have to do with a low signal-to-noise ratio (tSNR) in data from the EC.
claims.source: Previous studies postulated that the lack of univariate evidence of grid-like code may have to do with a low signal-to-noise ratio (tSNR) in data from the EC (Bao et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about previous literature, citing Bao et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Analysis revealed lower tSNR in all four entorhinal subregions compared to the frontal pole cluster from the quadrature filter analysis.
claims.source: Indeed, analysis ('Materials and methods') revealed lower tSNR in all four entorhinal subregions compared to the frontal pole cluster from the quadrature filter analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from tSNR analysis, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 5A.

claims.claim: The study did not identify a significant relationship between tSNR and the Z-transformed F statistics of hexagonal modulation either across participants or within participants.
claims.source: But we did not identify a significant relationship between tSNR and the Z-transformed F statistics of hexagonal modulation either across participants or within participants (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B and C, Table 4).
claims.evidence: This is a result from correlation analysis, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 5B and C, and Table 4.

claims.claim: The study cannot conclude that a low signal-to-noise ratio in EC led to the null finding.
claims.source: Thus, we cannot conclude that a low signal-to-noise ratio in EC led to this null finding in our study.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the tSNR analysis results.

claims.claim: The study provided some incomplete evidence of grid-like activity in the EC and prefrontal region while participants were mentally trespassing an abstract social space.
claims.source: Nonetheless, our study did provide some incomplete evidence of grid-like activity in the EC and prefrontal region while participants were mentally trespassing an abstract social space.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement in the Discussion.

claims.claim: Grid codes are proposed to provide a metric of space.
claims.source: Grid codes are proposed to provide a metric of space (Moser and Moser, 2008) and underlie the process of path integration (McNaughton et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical role of grid codes, with citations to Moser and Moser, 2008 and McNaughton et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Grid codes underlie the process of path integration.
claims.source: Grid codes are proposed to provide a metric of space (Moser and Moser, 2008) and underlie the process of path integration (McNaughton et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical role of grid codes, with citations to Moser and Moser, 2008 and McNaughton et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Entorhinal grid codes are capable of representing space at a higher level of abstraction that goes beyond spatial navigation to support cognitive flexibility in general.
claims.source: Previous studies have suggested that entorhinal grid codes are capable of representing space even at a higher level of abstraction that goes beyond spatial navigation to support cognitive flexibility in general (Bellmund et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about previous literature, citing Bellmund et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Existing literature revealed correlation between entorhinal and prefrontal grid-like code and performance in spatial, perceptual, and conceptual space.
claims.source: Existing literature revealed correlation between entorhinal and prefrontal grid-like code and performance in spatial, perceptual, and conceptual space.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of existing literature.

claims.claim: The univariate hexagonal consistency effect in temporal lobe scaled with the distance effect in a comparison task block when participants chose their preferred partner for future cooperation.
claims.source: Indeed, our exploratory analysis showed that the univariate hexagonal consistency effect in temporal lobe scaled with the distance effect in a comparison task block when participants chose their preferred partner for future cooperation.
claims.evidence: This is a result from exploratory analysis.

claims.claim: The distance effect reflected the extent to which participants relied on their preference judgment on the pairwise distance between the given pair of avatars.
claims.source: The distance effect reflected the extent to which participants relied on their preference judgment on the pairwise distance between the given pair of avatars.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the distance effect measure.

claims.claim: Park et al., 2021 found that the entorhinal and hippocampus system successfully reconstruct the unseen whole spectrum of social hierarchies as a 2D cognitive map.
claims.source: Replicating their previous findings (Park et al., 2020), the authors found that the entorhinal and hippocampus system successfully reconstruct the unseen whole spectrum of social hierarchies as a 2D cognitive map.
claims.evidence: This is a description of findings from Park et al., 2021 and Park et al., 2020.

results.result: The authors designed a 2D social value map defined by two orthogonal dimensions (competence and trustworthiness) with the same scale, operationalized through an investment game framework. Six avatars were placed on this map to serve as landmarks.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C19, C95-C96 describe the experimental design of the social value map. The operational definitions are clearly stated, the orthogonality and scale matching are explicit design choices, and the placement of avatars is documented. This is a methodological result that is well-supported by the experimental setup.

results.result: Participants successfully learned the social value map structure, as evidenced by improved performance across training sessions, accurate map reconstruction, distance effects in comparison tasks, and learning-induced changes in avatar ratings.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C28 provide converging behavioral evidence that participants formed an internal representation of the social value map. Statistical tests show significant improvements across sessions (p<0.001), distance effects in comparison tasks (p<0.001), and dissociable ratings post-learning (p<0.001). The multiple behavioral measures provide strong support for successful learning.

results.result: Neural distance coding during social navigation was identified, with bilateral precuneus showing positive correlation with traveled Euclidean distance, while bilateral fusiform gyrus and right middle occipital gyrus showed negative correlations.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 report distance coding results, but C29 notes only 'marginally significant' clusters in precuneus (p=0.056 and p=0.058 FWE-corrected). While the negative correlations in fusiform and MOG reached significance, the marginal significance of the primary positive finding and lack of clear interpretation for the negative correlations (acknowledged by authors) weaken the overall support.

results.result: Grid-like activity patterns with sixfold periodicity were found in vmPFC and left EC aligned to right frontal pole grid orientation, and in vmPFC and right superior temporal pole aligned to right pmEC grid orientation.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35, C44-C47, C61-C62 report significant grid consistency effects in multiple brain regions with appropriate statistical corrections (cluster-level p<0.05 FWE-corrected). The sixfold specificity was confirmed through control analyses (C42-C43). While not all predicted regions showed effects, the positive findings are statistically robust.

results.result: The study failed to find reliable evidence of grid-like code in the entorhinal cortex aligned to its own putative grid orientation using both univariate and multivariate approaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37, C67 consistently report null findings for EC grid-like activity aligned to its own orientation. This negative result is clearly stated and was tested with multiple approaches (univariate and RSA), making it a well-documented null finding. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation.

results.result: Voxel-wise grid orientations showed clustered distribution within ROIs for most participants in frontal pole, with less consistent results in pmEC. Grid orientations across participants distributed uniformly in right FP but not consistently in pmEC.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C41 report statistical tests (V-test, Rayleigh's test) of grid orientation distributions. The FP results are consistent (all p<0.011 except one participant), while pmEC shows mixed results (31/38 participants significant). The statistical tests are appropriate and results are clearly reported with their limitations.

results.result: Sixfold periodicity showed greater alignment effect compared to controlled periodicities (fourfold, fivefold, sevenfold, eightfold), with no modulation by control periodicities.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C43 report specificity controls for the grid-like findings. One-sample and paired t-tests confirmed sixfold specificity. This is an important control analysis that strengthens the interpretation of the grid-like findings as genuinely hexagonal rather than reflecting other periodicities.

results.result: Hexagonal consistency effect in temporal lobe regions (middle temporal gyrus, lingual gyrus) correlated with distance effect in the comparison task when participants chose preferred cooperation partners.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51, C77 report significant correlations between grid-like activity and behavioral performance (cluster-level p<0.001 or p<0.032 FWE-corrected). This provides evidence for behavioral relevance of the neural codes, though the left lingual result for pmEC orientation was marginal (p=0.077).

results.result: The intensity of hexagonal modulation in precuneus aligned to prefrontal grid orientation negatively correlated with social avoidance trait scores.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C83 report a correlation between grid-like activity and social avoidance scores. The finding is statistically significant (cluster-level p<0.001 FWE-corrected) and represents a novel link between grid-like codes and social functioning, though the authors acknowledge (C86-C87) that no grid-like pattern was found in precuneus itself.

results.result: No correlation was found between hexagonal modulation effect and accuracy in the recall task in the scanner, contrary to previous studies.
results.evaluation: Claim C48 reports a null finding with reference to prior literature (Constantinescu et al., 2016). This is a clearly documented negative result that differs from previous findings, appropriately reported as a limitation or difference from prior work.

results.result: While tSNR was lower in entorhinal subregions compared to frontal pole, no significant relationship was found between tSNR and hexagonal modulation effect, suggesting low signal-to-noise ratio does not explain the null EC findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 report tSNR analysis results. The lower tSNR in EC is documented (C69), but the lack of correlation between tSNR and hexagonal modulation (C70) is clearly stated with appropriate statistical tests. The conclusion (C71) appropriately reflects the data limitations.

results.result: The precuneus distance coding findings coincide with previous studies showing precuneus represents distance in social and spatial domains, suggesting a general role in encoding route distance.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 compare current findings to prior literature. While C56-C58 accurately cite previous work, C59 is explicitly speculative ('we speculate'). The interpretation extends beyond the data, and the marginal significance of the precuneus findings (p=0.056-0.058) weakens the comparison.

results.result: The study partly replicated previous findings of grid-like codes in prefrontal regions but not EC. The lack of evidence for grid cells in PFC suggests the observed codes likely reflect coordination between anatomically connected PFC and EC rather than local grid cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C66 provide interpretation of the grid-like findings in context of prior literature. The partial replication is accurately stated (C60), citations to prior work are appropriate (C63-C64), and the proposed explanation (C66) is reasonable given the anatomical connectivity literature cited, though explicitly speculative.

results.result: The study demonstrates that navigating continuous social space recruits distance and grid-like codes in brain regions associated with spatial navigation, supporting a domain-general role for spatial cognitive map mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92 represent the main conclusions. While behavioral learning is well-supported and some neural codes were found, the marginal significance of distance coding (p=0.056-0.058), absence of EC self-aligned grid codes, and mixed consistency of findings across regions weaken the strength of the overall conclusion. The evidence is suggestive but incomplete.

results.result: The study acknowledges limitations including potential confounding of sensory and abstract processing due to visual analogs, lack of social interaction in the task, and simplified orthogonal 2D design that may lack generality.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C97 explicitly acknowledge study limitations. These are appropriately identified methodological constraints that affect interpretation. The authors correctly note these as limitations rather than claiming the design is without constraints.

results.result: The authors discuss that real-world social cognitive maps may be nonuniform, high-dimensional, and have non-orthonormal dimensions, unlike the simplified experimental design, and suggest future studies should explore beyond sixfold periodicity in regular 2D space.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C111 provide extensive discussion of limitations and future directions. These are appropriately speculative statements about the nature of real-world social cognition, supported by relevant citations (C99-C100, C102-C103, C107-C108). The recommendations for future work (C111) are reasonable given the acknowledged limitations.

results.result: The study included 38 participants (from initial 44) after excluding 3 for excessive head motion and 3 for low behavioral accuracy, with appropriate ethical approval.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C116 describe the participant sample and exclusions. The exclusion criteria are clearly stated and reasonable (head motion >3mm, accuracy <60%). The final sample size (n=38) is comparable to previous fMRI studies in this domain. Ethical approval is documented.

results.result: Participants successfully learned to navigate the social value map, as evidenced by improved performance across training sessions, successful reconstruction of avatar layouts, and behavioral measures showing learning effects (claims C3, C20-C28).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the behavioral learning results. The first reviewer acknowledged 'a solid analysis revealed characteristic grid-like patterns associated with decision-making directions,' implicitly accepting the behavioral foundation. The third reviewer stated 'the experiment is designed appropriately' and noted 'a large amount of behavioral training per participant,' indicating acceptance of the behavioral training and learning outcomes.

results.result: Distance representation was identified in precuneus (positive correlation with traveled distance) and bilateral fusiform gyrus and right middle occipital gyrus (negative correlation with traveled distance) during navigation in social space (claims C4, C29-C31, C53-C56).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question the distance coding findings. The third reviewer explicitly stated 'They revealed that a number of brain regions correlated positively or negatively with distance in the social space,' directly affirming these results. No concerns were raised about the distance representation analysis or findings.

results.result: Partial evidence of grid-like representation patterns was found in medial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and entorhinal cortex (EC), with sixfold-specific grid-like codes aligned to frontal pole and posterior medial EC grid orientations (claims C5, C32-C35, C44-C47, C60-C62, C72).
results.evaluation: Reviewers expressed significant uncertainty about the grid-like findings. The first reviewer stated 'it remains uncertain whether these effects are genuinely due to navigating a conceptual social space or potentially confounded by changes in visual stimuli.' The second reviewer noted 'the observed grid-like neural activity might not signify navigating a social landscape but rather a sensory feature space.' The third reviewer acknowledged findings 'in line with prior findings' but emphasized that 'the problem is that, when the space is not a uniform, square/circular space, and 2-dimensional then there is no reason the code will be perfectly grid like.' The authors themselves acknowledged providing only 'partial' or 'incomplete' evidence.

results.result: The study did not identify reliable grid-like patterns in the entorhinal cortex aligned to its own grid orientation using either univariate or multivariate approaches (claims C36, C37, C67).
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged this null finding without disputing it. The third reviewer noted 'the current paper seems quite similar conceptually and in design to previous work' and discussed limitations of detecting grid codes in non-uniform spaces, implicitly accepting the null EC findings as consistent with theoretical expectations for complex social spaces.

results.result: The intensity of grid-like response scaled with navigation performance and social avoidance trait scores, with hexagonal consistency effects in temporal and lingual regions correlating with distance effects in behavioral tasks (claims C6, C7, C49-C51, C77, C83).
results.evaluation: While reviewers did not explicitly challenge these correlational findings, the broader uncertainty about whether grid-like patterns reflect true social navigation versus sensory processing (raised by reviewers 1 and 2) casts doubt on the interpretation of these behavioral correlations. The second reviewer questioned 'whether participants were actually traversing a social space mentally or simply recalling the bar graphs,' which undermines confidence in correlations between neural patterns and purported social navigation behavior.

results.result: The authors acknowledge multiple limitations: the visual analog may confound sensory and social processing; the task involves static social space without interaction; the orthogonal 2D design may lack generality; real social spaces may be nonuniform, high-dimensional, and have non-orthonormal dimensions (claims C93-C111).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorsed these limitations. The first reviewer stated 'it remains uncertain whether these effects are genuinely due to navigating a conceptual social space or potentially confounded by changes in visual stimuli.' The second reviewer emphasized 'the task did not necessitate any social cognitive processing' and that 'the space represented may be more perceptual than social in nature.' The third reviewer noted 'the problem is that, when the space is not a uniform, square/circular space, and 2-dimensional then there is no reason the code will be perfectly grid like' and stated 'After revision, the authors now discuss some of this and the limitations.'

results.result: The study demonstrates that navigating continuous social space recruits distance and grid-like codes in brain regions associated with spatial navigation, supporting the notion that spatial cognitive map mechanisms play a domain-general role in abstract knowledge representation (claims C91, C92).
results.evaluation: Reviewers questioned this main conclusion. The first reviewer stated the findings offer only 'partial support' and noted 'it remains uncertain whether these effects are genuinely due to navigating a conceptual social space.' The second reviewer argued 'the observed grid-like neural activity might not signify navigating a social landscape but rather a sensory feature space.' The third reviewer stated 'This data does specifically not add anything new to this argument' regarding evidence for spatial codes in abstract knowledge, emphasizing that the 2D orthogonal design does not generalize to real-world social spaces.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluations support the behavioral learning results (C20-C28). OpenEval provides detailed statistical evidence (p<0.001 across multiple measures), while peer reviewers implicitly accepted these findings without challenge, noting 'solid analysis' and 'appropriate' experimental design.

Both address distance coding (C29-C31, C53-C55). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to marginal significance (p=0.056-0.058) and unclear interpretation of negative correlations. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, explicitly affirming 'brain regions correlated positively or negatively with distance' without raising concerns about marginal significance.

Both evaluate grid-like findings (C32-C35, C44-C47, C61-C62). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on statistical robustness (p<0.05 FWE-corrected) and sixfold specificity controls. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, questioning whether effects reflect true social navigation versus sensory/visual confounds, and noting theoretical concerns about grid codes in non-uniform spaces.

Perfect agreement on null EC findings (C36-C37, C67). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes this as a 'well-documented null finding' tested with multiple approaches. Peer reviewers accept this result as consistent with theoretical expectations for complex social spaces.

Both address brain-behavior correlations (C49-C51, C77). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED based on significant correlations (p<0.001-0.032 FWE-corrected). Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, not challenging the statistical findings directly but questioning their interpretation given broader doubts about whether neural patterns reflect true social navigation versus sensory processing.

Both evaluate social avoidance correlations (C6-C7, C83). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED (p<0.001 FWE-corrected). Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, with the same interpretive concerns as R8/R5: statistical findings not disputed, but meaning questioned due to uncertainty about whether grid-like patterns reflect social versus sensory processing.

Both evaluate main conclusions (C91-C92). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, citing marginal distance coding significance, absent EC codes, and mixed findings. Peer reviewers also rate as UNCERTAIN, questioning whether effects reflect genuine social navigation and emphasizing the 2D orthogonal design doesn't generalize to real-world social spaces.

Both address study limitations (C93-C97 in R15; C93-C111 in R6). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting authors appropriately acknowledge methodological constraints. Peer reviewers also rate as SUPPORTED, explicitly endorsing these limitations and noting 'After revision, the authors now discuss some of this and the limitations.'

Both evaluate limitations and future directions (C98-C111). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, finding the discussion appropriately speculative with relevant citations. Peer reviewers also rate as SUPPORTED, with substantial overlap in the specific limitations emphasized (visual confounds, lack of social cognitive processing requirements, non-uniform space concerns).

OpenEval evaluated experimental design and operational definitions (C16-C19, C95-C96) as SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though peer reviewers did note the experiment was 'designed appropriately' in their general comments.

OpenEval evaluated grid orientation statistical tests (C38-C41) as SUPPORTED, noting appropriate use of V-test and Rayleigh's test with mixed results across regions. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval evaluated sixfold specificity controls (C42-C43) as SUPPORTED, noting these strengthen interpretation of hexagonal patterns. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though this relates to the grid-like findings peer reviewers questioned in R3.

OpenEval evaluated null finding regarding prior literature (C48) as SUPPORTED, noting clear documentation of negative result differing from Constantinescu et al. 2016. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
OpenEval evaluated tSNR analysis (C69-C71) as SUPPORTED, noting lower EC tSNR but lack of correlation with hexagonal modulation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval evaluated comparison to prior literature (C56-C59) as UNCERTAIN due to explicit speculation and marginal precuneus findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though C56 overlaps with distance coding claims peer reviewers accepted.

OpenEval evaluated interpretation of grid-like findings in literature context (C60, C63-C66) as SUPPORTED, noting accurate statements about partial replication and reasonable speculation about anatomical connectivity. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though C60 relates to grid findings peer reviewers questioned.
OpenEval evaluated participant sample and exclusions (C112-C116) as SUPPORTED, noting clear criteria and appropriate sample size. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.
